4. Thread Communication

Inter-thread communication is how threads exchange data and coordinate execution. There are four core strategies — pipes, shared memory, signaling, and message passing — and they differ in coupling, safety, and performance. BlockingQueue gets its own section because it is the most practical concurrency utility in the JVM world and it underlies Android's own work queues.

Table of Contents

  1. 4.1 Pipes
  2. 4.2 Shared Memory
  3. 4.3 Signaling
    • wait / notify
    • CountDownLatch
    • Semaphore
    • CyclicBarrier
    • Mutex (ReentrantLock)
    • Condition Variables
    • CountDownLatch vs Semaphore
    • Signal vs Shared Data
  4. 4.4 BlockingQueue
  5. 4.5 Message Passing — Android Handler/Looper/MessageQueue
  6. Cross-cutting: Shared Memory vs Message Passing

4.1 Pipes

Definition

A pipe is a unidirectional, buffer-backed channel that connects exactly two threads: a producer writes into the write-end and a consumer reads from the read-end. The channel owns a fixed internal buffer, and the JVM manages flow control automatically — the producer blocks when the buffer is full and the consumer blocks when it is empty.

In Java/Kotlin the standard classes are:

  • PipedOutputStream / PipedInputStream — byte streams
  • PipedWriter / PipedReader — character streams
fun pipeExample() {
    val writer = PipedWriter()
    val reader = PipedReader(writer)   // connects the two ends

    // Producer thread
    Thread {
        writer.use { w ->
            w.write("hello from producer\n")
        }
    }.start()

    // Consumer thread
    Thread {
        reader.use { r ->
            val buf = CharArray(256)
            val n = r.read(buf)
            println(String(buf, 0, n))   // "hello from producer"
        }
    }.start()
}

Internals

  1. PipedWriter.connect(PipedReader) links both ends to a shared circular char buffer (default

1024 chars / 1024 bytes for the byte variant).

  1. Write side: if the buffer is full the producer blocks (wait()) until the consumer drains

some data.

  1. Read side: if the buffer is empty the consumer blocks until the producer writes more data or

closes the write-end (EOF).

  1. Closing the write-end signals EOF to the reader.
  2. Broken pipe: if the reader thread dies, the next producer write throws

IOException("Pipe broken").

Blocking Behavior and Thread-Design Implications

Condition What happens Thread impact
Buffer fullProducer blocks on write()Producer thread is descheduled; no busy-wait
Buffer emptyConsumer blocks on read()Consumer thread is descheduled
Write-end closedread() returns -1 (EOF)Consumer can exit cleanly
Reader thread deadwrite() throws IOExceptionProducer must handle exception

Because both ends block, the two threads must run on separate threads — connecting both ends on the same thread is a classic deadlock: the producer fills the buffer and blocks before the consumer ever gets CPU time.

Pipelines

Multiple pipes can be chained:

Thread-A --> PipedWriter/Reader --> Thread-B --> PipedWriter/Reader --> Thread-C

This is analogous to Unix cmd1 | cmd2 | cmd3. Each intermediate thread is both a consumer (of the upstream pipe) and a producer (of the downstream pipe).

Android Implications

PipedInputStream/OutputStream are standard Java and work on Android, but they are rarely used in modern Android code. The more idiomatic equivalents are:

  • Kotlin Channel<T> — typed, suspending, composable with coroutines.
  • Flow — cold, lazy pipe that only runs when collected.
  • SharedFlow / StateFlow — hot variants for multi-subscriber broadcast.

Use java.io.Pipe* only when you must interface with legacy InputStream/OutputStream APIs.

Trade-offs

Pro Con
Simple producer→consumer couplingOnly byte/char streams (no typed objects)
Natural backpressure (buffer full → block)Must be on separate threads
EOF signals termination cleanlyBroken-pipe if consumer dies
No explicit lock management1 KB default buffer; may need tuning

Failure Modes

  • Deadlock: both ends on the same thread.
  • Broken pipe: consumer thread dies; producer gets IOException.
  • Starvation: consumer is too slow and producer keeps blocking — pipeline throughput limited by slowest stage.

Interview Angles

What is a pipe?

"A pipe is a unidirectional, buffer-backed byte or character channel between exactly two threads. The producer blocks when the buffer is full; the consumer blocks when it is empty. That blocking behavior is actually the feature — it gives you natural backpressure without any manual synchronization."

When would pipe-style communication be useful?

"Pipes are most useful for streaming data processing — things like log parsing, transcoding, or compression pipelines — where you want natural backpressure and you don't want to write manual synchronization. They're also the right tool when you need to interface with legacy APIs that speak InputStream or OutputStream, because those APIs expect a stream, and a pipe gives you exactly that."

How does blocking affect thread design?

"The key constraint is that each end of the pipe must live on its own thread, because blocking puts the thread to sleep — no busy-wait — but it also means that thread is stuck waiting. So you need one thread per pipeline stage. In modern Android the better answer is to replace pipes with Channel<T> from coroutines, which suspends instead of blocking, so many logical stages can share a small thread pool without starving each other."

4.2 Shared Memory

Definition

Shared memory is the default communication model in Java and Kotlin — all threads share the heap, so any thread can read or write the same field directly without copying anything. That zero-copy access is what makes it fast, but it also means every concurrent read-write pair is a potential race condition unless you establish a happens-before relationship.

// Unsynchronized shared counter — DATA RACE
class SharedCounter {
    var count = 0         // shared mutable state
}

val counter = SharedCounter()
val t1 = Thread { repeat(100_000) { counter.count++ } }
val t2 = Thread { repeat(100_000) { counter.count++ } }
t1.start(); t2.start()
t1.join();  t2.join()
// counter.count is NOT reliably 200_000

Synchronization Need

The JVM memory model (JMM, JSR-133) does not guarantee that writes by one thread are immediately visible to another unless a happens-before relationship exists. Happens-before is established by:

  • synchronized block/method entry and exit
  • volatile write → subsequent volatile read
  • Thread.start() → first action in that thread
  • Thread.join() → actions after join see all writes before join
  • Lock.unlock() → subsequent Lock.lock()

Without happens-before, a thread may see a stale cached value from its CPU register or L1 cache.

Race Conditions

A race condition occurs when the correctness of the program depends on the relative timing of thread scheduling. The classic example is check-then-act:

// BAD: check-then-act without atomicity
if (map.containsKey(key)) {          // check
    val v = map[key]!!               // act — another thread may have removed key here
    process(v)
}

Read-modify-write is another common pattern:

// count++ is actually: read count, add 1, write count — three non-atomic steps
counter.count++

Visibility Issues

@Volatile on a JVM field forces every read/write to go to main memory (disables CPU caching of that field) and prevents instruction reordering around it:

@Volatile var running = true        // other threads see the update immediately

// Writer thread
fun stop() { running = false }

// Reader thread
while (running) { /* work */ }      // will observe running=false without @Volatile delay

@Volatile solves visibility but not atomicity. running = false is a single write, so @Volatile is sufficient. count++ (read-modify-write) still needs AtomicInteger or synchronized.

Protecting Shared Mutable State

Mechanism Use-case Cost
synchronized blockcoarse-grained critical sectionmoderate (monitor acquire/release)
ReentrantLocksame as synchronized but with tryLock / timed lockmoderate
AtomicInteger / AtomicReferencesingle-field CASvery low (single CAS instruction)
@Volatilesingle boolean flag / referencevery low (memory barrier)
ConcurrentHashMapthread-safe map readslow (striped locking)
Immutable datano writes → no raceszero (allocation cost only)
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger

class SafeCounter {
    private val count = AtomicInteger(0)
    fun increment() = count.incrementAndGet()
    fun get() = count.get()
}

Immutability Reduces Risk

An immutable object's state cannot change after construction. Any thread can read it freely because there are no concurrent writes to race with. In Kotlin, prefer:

  • val over var wherever possible.
  • data class with all val fields — a classic value object.
  • Kotlin's List / Map / Set (read-only views) for collections.
  • copy() to produce new instances with modified fields.
data class Config(val host: String, val port: Int)   // immutable; safe to share across threads

When state must change, use the replace pattern: create a new immutable instance and swap an AtomicReference:

val configRef = AtomicReference(Config("localhost", 8080))

// thread-safe update
configRef.updateAndGet { old -> old.copy(port = 9090) }

Android Implications

  • Main thread holds View state. Only the main thread should read/write View properties.

Background threads communicating results to the UI must go through LiveData, StateFlow, or Handler.post.

  • ViewModel is often accessed from both background coroutines and the UI thread. Use

MutableStateFlow (which is thread-safe) instead of raw mutable fields.

  • Room handles its own internal locking; never hold a Cursor across threads.

Trade-offs

Pro Con
Zero-copy — extremely fastRequires explicit synchronization
Familiar Java modelDeadlock risk if locks acquired in different order
Fine-grained controlRace conditions are silent and hard to reproduce
Works well for small hot dataVisibility bugs are compiler/CPU dependent

Failure Modes

  • Data race: two threads write/write or read/write the same field without synchronization —

undefined behavior under the JMM.

  • Stale read: a thread caches a field value in a register; writes from other threads are never

observed.

  • Deadlock: thread A holds lock-1 and waits for lock-2; thread B holds lock-2 and waits for

lock-1.

  • Livelock: threads keep reacting to each other but make no forward progress.
  • Priority inversion: a high-priority thread waits for a lock held by a low-priority thread

that is itself starved by a medium-priority thread.

4.3 Signaling

Signaling is about threads notifying each other — "I am done", "a slot is available", "N workers have reached the rendezvous" — and it is distinct from sharing data. You can signal without transferring any payload at all.

wait/notify

wait/notify is the lowest-level JVM signaling mechanism. Every object has an intrinsic monitor, and a thread that holds that monitor can call wait() to release it and suspend. Another thread then calls notify() or notifyAll() to wake the waiting thread or threads back up.

val lock = Object()
var ready = false

// Consumer thread
Thread {
    synchronized(lock) {
        while (!ready) {         // always loop — spurious wakeups
            lock.wait()
        }
        println("Consumer: data is ready")
    }
}.start()

// Producer thread
Thread {
    Thread.sleep(500)
    synchronized(lock) {
        ready = true
        lock.notify()            // wake one waiter
    }
}.start()

Rules:

  1. wait() / notify() must be called from within a synchronized block on the same object.
  2. Always check the condition in a while loop, not if — spurious wakeups are permitted by

the JVM spec.

  1. notify() wakes one arbitrary waiter; notifyAll() wakes all — safer when multiple threads

wait for different conditions.

Limitations: wait/notify is fragile, verbose, and hard to compose. In practice you should always prefer the higher-level utilities below.

CountDownLatch

A CountDownLatch lets one or more threads wait until a set of operations in other threads completes. You initialize it with a count; each worker calls countDown() when it finishes; and any waiter calls await(), which blocks until the count reaches zero.

Key property: one-shot, non-resettable.

import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch

fun parallelInit() {
    val latch = CountDownLatch(3)   // 3 workers to wait for

    repeat(3) { i ->
        Thread {
            println("Worker $i initializing...")
            Thread.sleep(100L * (i + 1))
            println("Worker $i done")
            latch.countDown()       // decrement
        }.start()
    }

    latch.await()                   // main thread blocks here until count == 0
    println("All workers done, proceeding")
}

Timed variant: latch.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) returns false if it times out.

Android use: waiting for multiple parallel API calls before showing a screen; waiting for analytics SDK init before logging events.

Semaphore

A Semaphore maintains a count of permits. acquire() decrements the count and blocks if it is already zero; release() increments it. The whole point is to control how many threads can access a bounded resource pool at the same time.

import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore

val dbConnections = Semaphore(5)    // max 5 concurrent DB connections

fun queryDatabase(query: String) {
    dbConnections.acquire()         // blocks if 5 connections already in use
    try {
        // use the connection
        println("Executing: $query")
        Thread.sleep(200)
    } finally {
        dbConnections.release()     // always release, even on exception
    }
}

Binary semaphore (permits=1): behaves like a mutex, but with two important differences — it is not re-entrant, and it can be released by a different thread than the one that acquired it. That is unlike synchronized, which is re-entrant and is always released by its owning thread.

Fair semaphore: Semaphore(n, true) grants permits in FIFO order, preventing starvation.

Android use: throttling parallel image downloads; limiting concurrent network requests.

CyclicBarrier

A CyclicBarrier makes N threads rendezvous at a common point. Each thread calls await(); the last one to arrive optionally triggers a barrier action, and then all threads are released together. The key difference from CountDownLatch is that a CyclicBarrier is resettable — you can reuse it for multiple phases of work.

import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier

val barrier = CyclicBarrier(3) {
    println("All 3 threads reached the barrier — next phase begins")
}

repeat(3) { i ->
    Thread {
        println("Thread $i doing phase 1 work")
        Thread.sleep(50L * (i + 1))
        barrier.await()             // wait for all peers
        println("Thread $i doing phase 2 work")
    }.start()
}

Android use: coordinating multiple parallel data-fetch coroutines before merging results (more idiomatic: awaitAll() in coroutines).

Mutex / ReentrantLock

ReentrantLock is the explicit-lock equivalent of synchronized. "Re-entrant" means the same thread can lock it multiple times without deadlocking — it just keeps an internal acquisition count and only releases when that count drops to zero.

import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock

val lock = ReentrantLock()

fun criticalSection() {
    lock.lock()
    try {
        // protected code
    } finally {
        lock.unlock()   // must always be in finally
    }
}

// Timed tryLock — avoids deadlock by giving up
fun tryWork(): Boolean {
    if (lock.tryLock(100, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
        try {
            // do work
            return true
        } finally {
            lock.unlock()
        }
    }
    return false   // could not acquire lock in time
}

Kotlin coroutines provide kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex — a suspending mutex that does not block a thread. When one coroutine holds it, others suspend rather than park their OS thread:

import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex
import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withLock

val mutex = Mutex()

suspend fun safeUpdate() {
    mutex.withLock {
        // only one coroutine runs this at a time
    }
}

Condition Variables

A Condition is associated with a Lock and lets you have multiple wait queues on a single lock. That is something plain synchronized cannot do — every synchronized object has only one wait-set, so you cannot separately signal "not full" and "not empty". With two Condition objects you can.

import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock

val lock = ReentrantLock()
val notEmpty = lock.newCondition()
val notFull  = lock.newCondition()
val buffer = ArrayDeque<Int>()
val capacity = 10

fun produce(value: Int) {
    lock.lock()
    try {
        while (buffer.size == capacity) notFull.await()
        buffer.addLast(value)
        notEmpty.signal()
    } finally { lock.unlock() }
}

fun consume(): Int {
    lock.lock()
    try {
        while (buffer.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await()
        val v = buffer.removeFirst()
        notFull.signal()
        return v
    } finally { lock.unlock() }
}

This pattern is exactly how LinkedBlockingQueue is implemented internally.

CountDownLatch vs Semaphore

Dimension CountDownLatch Semaphore
PurposeWait for N events to completeThrottle concurrent access to a resource
ResettableNo — one-shotYes — release() can add permits at any time
DirectionWorkers decrement; waiters awaitAcquirers take permits; holders release
Who calls whatWorkers: countDown() / Waiters: await()Same threads: acquire() then release()
Permits > 0Any remaining count just means not all events happenedMultiple threads can proceed concurrently
Permits = 0All events done, all waiters releasedResource exhausted, all acquirers block
Android analogyWait for analytics + feature flags before showing first screenLimit parallel image downloads to 3

The rule of thumb is: reach for CountDownLatch when you want "wait until done", and reach for Semaphore when you want "allow at most N concurrent".

Signal vs Shared Data

When two threads need to communicate, there are two broad approaches — you signal the other thread, or you poll a shared flag — and the table below shows where each wins:

Signaling Polling shared data
Mechanismnotify(), CountDownLatch, Channel, FlowLoop checking a @Volatile flag
CPU useZero while waiting (thread sleeps)Burns CPU if spinning; moderate with sleep()
LatencyLow — woken immediatelyDepends on poll interval
ComplexityRequires synchronization protocolSimple but brittle
Missed signalsRisk if notify() fires before wait() — use condition loopN/A — flag stays set
VerdictPrefer for event-driven handoffsOnly for simple termination flags (@Volatile running)

Android Implications for Signaling

  • Prefer kotlinx.coroutines primitives (Mutex, Channel, Job.join(), async/await) over

Java concurrency utilities — they are suspending and work correctly with coroutine cancellation.

  • CountDownLatch.await() blocks the calling thread — never call it on the main thread.
  • Use Flow.first() or StateFlow as a coroutine-native alternative to CountDownLatch for

"wait for a value to become available".

4.4 BlockingQueue

Definition

A BlockingQueue<E> is a thread-safe queue that blocks the caller whenever the operation cannot complete immediately. There are two key operations: put(e) blocks if the queue is full until space becomes available, and take() blocks if the queue is empty until an element is added. That blocking contract is what makes it the foundational building block for the producer-consumer pattern — no manual wait/notify required.

Producer Thread(s)              BlockingQueue              Consumer Thread(s)
      |                      +------------------+                |
      |---- put(item) -----> |  [ ][ ][ ][ ]    | <-- take() ---|
      |  (blocks if full)    +------------------+  (blocks if empty)

Producer-Consumer Example

import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit

fun producerConsumerDemo() {
    val queue = LinkedBlockingQueue<Int>(5)    // bounded: max 5 items

    // Producer
    val producer = Thread {
        for (i in 1..10) {
            println("Producing $i")
            queue.put(i)                        // blocks when queue has 5 items
            Thread.sleep(50)
        }
        queue.put(-1)                           // sentinel: signals end-of-stream
    }

    // Consumer
    val consumer = Thread {
        while (true) {
            val item = queue.take()             // blocks when queue is empty
            if (item == -1) break
            println("Consuming $item (queue size: ${queue.size})")
            Thread.sleep(150)                   // consumer is slower than producer
        }
    }

    producer.start()
    consumer.start()
    producer.join()
    consumer.join()
}

Internals

LinkedBlockingQueue uses two separate ReentrantLocks — one guarding the head for takes, one guarding the tail for puts — plus two Condition variables (notEmpty, notFull). That "two-lock" design is what lets puts and takes happen simultaneously at full concurrency.

ArrayBlockingQueue uses a single lock instead, which is slightly lower throughput, but it pre-allocates its array so it uses less memory overall.

Implementation Backing Bounded? Notes
LinkedBlockingQueueLinked nodesOptional (default MAX_VALUE)High throughput (2 locks)
ArrayBlockingQueueArrayYes (required)Fair ordering option; lower GC pressure
PriorityBlockingQueueHeapUnboundedItems dequeued by priority, not FIFO
SynchronousQueueNo storageEffectively 0Each put blocks until a take, and vice versa
DelayQueueHeapUnboundedItems become available only after their delay

Blocking vs Non-Blocking Operations

Method Behavior
put(e)Blocks until space available
take()Blocks until element available
offer(e)Returns false immediately if full
poll()Returns null immediately if empty
offer(e, time, unit)Times out if still full after duration
poll(time, unit)Times out if still empty after duration

Bounded vs Unbounded Queues

Bounded queue (e.g., ArrayBlockingQueue(100) or LinkedBlockingQueue(100)):

  • Finite memory footprint — predictable and safe.
  • put() blocks when full, which gives you natural backpressure: producers automatically slow down when consumers fall behind.
  • Prevents OOM when consumers are slower than producers.

Unbounded queue (default LinkedBlockingQueue(), PriorityBlockingQueue):

  • put() never blocks (until heap memory is exhausted).
  • There is no backpressure — a fast producer and a slow consumer will grow the queue without limit.
  • Risk: OutOfMemoryError if the producer is consistently faster than the consumer.

Backpressure

Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow consumer signals to a fast producer to slow down. With a bounded BlockingQueue, backpressure is built-in — a full queue simply blocks the producer thread until the consumer processes some items, and no extra code is needed.

With an unbounded queue, you have to implement backpressure yourself. Two options: check queue.size and slow the producer when it crosses a threshold, or use a SynchronousQueue where every put must be matched by a take — zero buffering, maximum backpressure.

In Kotlin coroutines, Channel<T> with a finite capacity achieves the same effect with suspension instead of blocking.

Android Implications

  • ThreadPoolExecutor accepts a BlockingQueue<Runnable> as its work queue:
    • LinkedBlockingQueue (unbounded) — Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) default; can OOM.
    • SynchronousQueue — Executors.newCachedThreadPool() default; no buffering.
    • ArrayBlockingQueue(n) — explicit bound; execute() throws RejectedExecutionException when

full (useful for shedding load).

  • AsyncTask (deprecated) used an internal LinkedBlockingQueue.
  • Modern Android: prefer coroutine Channel or Flow with buffer() operator over raw

BlockingQueue in app code.

  • Never call take() or put() on the main thread — they block and cause ANR.

Trade-offs

Pro Con
Thread-safe by designtake()/put() block calling thread — must not call on main thread
Natural backpressure with bounded queueUnbounded queues risk OOM
Rich API (offer, poll, timed variants)FIFO ordering only (unless PriorityBlockingQueue)
Decouples producer and consumer speedsSentinel-value pattern is fragile (what if producer dies?)

Failure Modes

  • Unbounded queue OOM: production system — always use bounded queues in production.
  • Lost sentinel: producer crashes before sending the "poison pill" (-1, null, etc.) →

consumer blocks forever. Mitigate: use timed poll() with a timeout, or use Future/ CompletableFuture to model completion.

  • Thread starvation: too few consumer threads for the volume; queue backs up.
  • Deadlock: two BlockingQueues where thread A waits on queue-1 and thread B waits on

queue-2, while each holds the other.

Interview Angles

Why use BlockingQueue?

"A BlockingQueue separates producers from consumers with a thread-safe buffer and gives you automatic blocking semantics — no manual wait/notify needed. The bounded variant goes one step further and gives you free backpressure: a full queue automatically slows the producer without any extra code on your part."

What happens with an unbounded queue?

"put() never blocks, all the way up until the heap is exhausted. If the producer is consistently faster than the consumer, the queue grows without limit and you eventually get an OutOfMemoryError. That is why I always use a bounded queue in production systems where load is unpredictable — an unbounded queue is essentially a memory leak waiting to happen."

How do you implement backpressure?

"The simplest answer is to use a bounded BlockingQueue — the producer's put() naturally blocks when the queue is full, which is backpressure by definition. If you need something softer, use offer(e, timeout, unit) and apply back-off or drop logic when it times out. And in coroutines, Channel with a finite capacity does the same thing with suspension instead of blocking."

4.5 Message Passing — Android Handler/Looper/MessageQueue

Definition

Message passing is a communication model where threads exchange discrete, self-contained messages rather than sharing mutable state. The sender packages data into a message and dispatches it into a queue; the receiver picks it up and processes it on its own thread. The key point is that threads never directly touch each other's memory — data is owned by one thread at a time and transferred via the message.

This is the model behind Erlang actors, Go channels, and Android's own Handler/Looper/MessageQueue system.

Avoids Shared Mutable State

Because each message is delivered to exactly one thread's queue and processed serially, there is never a concurrent read-write on the same data. Races are eliminated by design — not by adding locks, but because the ownership model makes them structurally impossible.

Thread A owns data-A         Thread B owns data-B
     |                             |
     |  Message { data copy }      |
     |----------------------------->
                                   | processes message serially
                                   | never races with Thread A

Android Handler/Looper/MessageQueue Architecture

Android's main thread has run inside a Looper loop since ActivityThread.main(). Every component lifecycle event — onCreate, onStart, button clicks, draw frames — is a Message or Runnable dispatched through the main MessageQueue. There is no special fast path; it all goes through the same queue.

           ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
           │           Main Thread                   │
           │                                         │
           │  Looper.loop()                          │
           │    └── MessageQueue.next()              │
           │          └── dequeue Message/Runnable   │
           │                └── Handler.dispatchMessage() │
           └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ▲
                              │  Handler.sendMessage() / post(Runnable)
                              │
           ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
           │         Background Thread               │
           └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Core Classes

Class Role
LooperOwns a MessageQueue; runs an infinite dequeue loop on its thread
MessageQueueThread-safe priority queue of Message objects, ordered by when timestamp
HandlerAPI for posting Message/Runnable to a Looper's queue; also processes them
MessageLightweight data carrier: what (int), obj (Object), arg1/arg2, data (Bundle)

Typical Background-to-Main Thread Communication

class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private val mainHandler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())

    fun startWork() {
        Thread {
            val result = fetchDataFromNetwork()   // runs on background thread
            mainHandler.post {
                // this Runnable runs on the main thread
                textView.text = result
            }
        }.start()
    }
}

Creating a Background Looper Thread

class WorkerThread : Thread("worker") {
    lateinit var handler: Handler
    private val ready = CountDownLatch(1)

    override fun run() {
        Looper.prepare()
        handler = Handler(Looper.myLooper()!!)
        ready.countDown()       // signal that handler is ready
        Looper.loop()           // blocks here; processes messages until quit()
    }

    fun start() = apply {
        super.start()
        ready.await()           // caller waits until Looper is set up
    }

    fun quit() = handler.looper.quit()
}

val worker = WorkerThread().start()
worker.handler.post { /* runs on WorkerThread */ }
worker.quit()

HandlerThread is Android's convenience wrapper that does exactly the above.

sendMessage vs post

// post: Runnable wrapped in a Message
handler.post { doWork() }

// sendMessage: structured message with type code
val msg = Message.obtain(handler, MSG_LOAD_DATA)
msg.arg1 = itemId
handler.sendMessage(msg)

// delayed
handler.postDelayed({ doWork() }, 2000L)
handler.sendMessageDelayed(msg, 2000L)

Messages Should Be Small

Message objects are pooled — Message.obtain() retrieves from a recycled pool to avoid allocation. Passing large objects (large bitmaps, deep object graphs) via Message.obj or Bundle is an anti-pattern for two reasons. First, it defeats the purpose of message passing, because you are really just sharing the same object reference, which reintroduces all the ownership and visibility problems you were trying to avoid. Second, large Bundles cause IPC overhead when crossing process boundaries via Binder. The right approach is to pass an identifier or a lightweight value object and let the consumer fetch the full data itself.

Message Ordering

MessageQueue orders messages by their when timestamp (wall-clock SystemClock.uptimeMillis()). Within the same delivery time, messages are processed FIFO. sendMessageAtFrontOfQueue() bypasses that ordering — use it sparingly, because it can starve other messages.

Two subtleties worth knowing: ordering is not guaranteed across different Handler instances even if they post to the same Looper, and Looper.myLooper().setMessageLogging() can measure dispatch times — which is the basis for BlockCanary and Choreographer jank detection.

Delayed-Message Lifecycle Leaks

Delayed messages are one of the most common sources of Android memory leaks:

// LEAKS the Activity
class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())

    override fun onCreate(...) {
        handler.postDelayed({
            // this lambda captures 'this' (MyActivity) implicitly
            updateUI()
        }, 30_000L)    // 30-second delay
    }
}

Why it leaks: The Message holds a reference to the Runnable lambda, and the lambda captures this — the Activity. The MessageQueue is owned by the Looper, which outlives the Activity, so the chain is: Looper → MessageQueue → Message → Runnable → Activity. That chain keeps the Activity from being garbage-collected for the full 30 seconds even after finish() is called.

Fix:

class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
    private val updateRunnable = Runnable { updateUI() }

    override fun onCreate(...) {
        handler.postDelayed(updateRunnable, 30_000L)
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        super.onDestroy()
        handler.removeCallbacks(updateRunnable)   // cancel pending message
    }
}

Or use a static inner class + WeakReference:

private class SafeRunnable(activity: MyActivity) : Runnable {
    private val ref = WeakReference(activity)
    override fun run() { ref.get()?.updateUI() }
}

Or, in modern Android: replace Handler.postDelayed with a coroutine:

override fun onCreate(...) {
    lifecycleScope.launch {
        delay(30_000L)
        updateUI()              // auto-cancelled when Activity is destroyed
    }
}

lifecycleScope is bound to the Lifecycle and is automatically cancelled on onDestroy — no manual cleanup needed at all.

Android Implications Summary

Pattern Tool Notes
Background → Main UI updateHandler(mainLooper).post {}Classic but verbose
Background → Main UI (modern)withContext(Dispatchers.Main) {}Coroutine; cleaner
Main → Background workHandler(HandlerThread.looper).post {}Works; prefer coroutines
Delayed work (no leak)lifecycleScope.launch { delay(…) }Lifecycle-aware cancellation
Inter-process messageBinder / AIDLBuilt on same Message model, IPC overhead
BroadcastBroadcastReceiverHeavyweight; use LocalBroadcastManager or Flow locally

Trade-offs

Pro Con
No shared mutable state → no racesMessage copying overhead (small)
Natural ordering via queueDelayed messages can cause lifecycle leaks
Decoupled sender/receiverVerbose boilerplate (Handler, Message.obtain, what codes)
Pooled Message objects reduce allocationLarge messages anti-pattern — tempting to pass big objects
Main-thread model is single-threaded serialQueue can back up if handler is slow (ANR risk)

Failure Modes

  • Lifecycle leak: delayed message holds Activity reference past onDestroy. Always call

removeCallbacks in onDestroy or use lifecycleScope.

  • Message queue overflow: main thread ANR if the queue backs up (>5 sec without processing).
  • Wrong Looper: calling Handler() without specifying Looper was deprecated in API 30

because it defaults to the calling thread's Looper, which may not be the main thread. Always pass Looper.getMainLooper() or a specific HandlerThread.looper explicitly.

  • Accessing destroyed context: Message.obj holds a reference to an Activity that is now

isDestroyed. Always guard: if (!isDestroyed) { … }.

Interview Angles

Shared memory vs message passing?

"Shared memory is fast — zero-copy, direct read-write — but it requires explicit synchronization to prevent races and visibility problems, and that synchronization is where bugs live. Message passing eliminates races by design: data is owned by one thread at a time, and transferring a message is a disciplined handoff, so there is nothing to race over. Android's Handler/Looper system is pure message passing for the main thread. The trade-off is that message passing adds a small amount of serialization overhead and queue latency, while shared memory adds synchronization complexity and risk. In practice I default to message passing for Android app code and only reach for shared memory when profiling shows the queue overhead is actually a bottleneck."

How does Android main-thread communication work?

"The main thread runs Looper.loop(), which just spins on MessageQueue.next(). Any other thread can create a Handler bound to Looper.getMainLooper() and post Message or Runnable objects into the main queue. The Looper dequeues them in when-timestamp order and dispatches each one to its Handler on the main thread. Every View callback, every lifecycle event, every touch event, and every Choreographer frame goes through that same queue — there is no other path onto the main thread."

How can delayed messages leak an Activity?

"The chain is: Handler.postDelayed(runnable, 30_000) stores the Runnable inside a Message in the MessageQueue. The MessageQueue is owned by the Looper, which is a long-lived process-level object. If the Runnable is a lambda inside the Activity, it implicitly captures this, so the full reference chain from Looper down to Activity is alive for the entire 30-second window. The Activity cannot be garbage-collected even after finish(). The fix has three options: call handler.removeCallbacks(runnable) in onDestroy, use a WeakReference so the chain doesn't keep the Activity alive, or replace the whole thing with a lifecycleScope.launch { delay(30_000) } coroutine that is automatically cancelled when the Activity is destroyed."

Cross-cutting: Shared Memory vs Message Passing

This comparison appears as an interview question in both 4.2 and 4.5.

Dimension Shared Memory Message Passing
Data transferBy reference (zero copy)By value or disciplined reference
SynchronizationExplicit (locks, atomics, volatile)Implicit (queue serializes access)
Race conditionsPossible — developer's responsibilityEliminated by design
Deadlock riskYes — if multiple locks acquiredLow — queues do not cross-lock
PerformanceFastest (direct read/write)Small overhead (queue ops, potential copy)
CouplingTight (both threads know the shared object)Loose (sender just posts; receiver owns)
OrderingNo inherent ordering guaranteesFIFO queue provides natural ordering
BackpressureManual (check and throttle)Natural (bounded queue blocks sender)
Android example@Volatile running, AtomicReference<Config>Handler.post {}, Channel, Flow
Best forHigh-frequency, low-latency data sharing (audio buffers, game state)Event-driven UI updates, actor-style isolation

The guideline is: default to message passing (coroutines + Channel/Flow) for new Android code. Reach for shared memory only when profiling shows the message overhead is an actual bottleneck, and always protect it with the minimum synchronization necessary.

End of Section 4: Thread Communication

5. IPC: Binder, AIDL, Messenger

Senior/staff-level Android interview study material. Every subtopic, interview angle, failure mode, and trade-off covered.

Table of Contents

  1. 5.1 Android Process Model
  2. 5.2 Binder
  3. 5.3 AIDL
  4. 5.4 Messenger
  5. Cross-Cutting: Parcelable vs Serializable
  6. Cross-Cutting: AIDL vs Messenger Decision Guide
  7. Interview Quick-Reference

5.1 Android Process Model

Definition

Every Android app runs in its own Linux process by default, completely isolated from every other app at the OS kernel level. That process hosts a Dalvik/ART VM, a main thread with its own Looper, a Binder thread pool, and the app's heap. The OS assigns each process a unique UID and PID.

How components map to processes

By default, all four component types (Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver, ContentProvider) declared in a single APK run in the same process — the one named after the app's package. You opt components into a different process via the android:process attribute:

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<service
    android:name=".AudioPlayerService"
    android:process=":audio" />   <!-- ':' prefix = private process, scoped to this app -->

<service
    android:name=".SyncService"
    android:process="com.example.sync" />  <!-- no ':' = shared process, any app with same UID -->

When components live in different processes, they share no memory at all — not the heap, not static fields, not singletons. The JVM runs a completely separate instance for every process. That's the fundamental reason IPC exists: you cannot pass an object reference across process boundaries.

Memory isolation

Scope Same process Different processes
Static variablesSharedNot shared — each process has its own copy
Singleton instancesSharedIndependent instances
Object referencesValid pointersMeaningless (different address space)
Files / SharedPreferencesShared if same UID and no MODE_PRIVATENeed ContentProvider or FileProvider

"What happens to static variables across processes?"

"Each process gets its own JVM, so a companion object or @JvmStatic field is initialized independently in every process. Changing the value in process A has zero effect on process B. This is a surprisingly common source of confusion when teams introduce a :remote service without realizing their in-memory cache now has two stale, independent copies."

Process lifecycle and death

The Android OS is free to kill any background process at any time to reclaim memory. The kill order follows a priority ladder — foreground, then visible, then service, then background, then empty — but the OS makes no guarantees beyond that ordering. A service running in a separate process can die while the app's UI is still alive, or vice versa.

There are three implications worth internalizing. First, any state stored only in static or instance memory is gone on process death. Second, if you hold a reference to a remote IBinder, the remote can disappear under you at any moment — you must handle RemoteException and register a death recipient (covered in §5.2). Third, bound services get a callback when the remote process dies: ServiceConnection.onServiceDisconnected.

Bound vs remote services

Type Same process Different process
Started servicestartService()startService() across packages, but still same process unless android:process set
Bound service (local)IBinder returned from onBind() is a direct object reference, no IPC overheadN/A
Bound service (remote)—onBind() returns an AIDL stub or Messenger; every call crosses a Binder transaction

The key insight is that binding to a service in another process is still bindService(), but Android transparently routes the IBinder through the Binder driver. The client receives a proxy object, not the real object.

Interview angles — process model

Q: Process vs thread?

"A process is an OS-level isolation unit — it has its own address space, its own PID, its own UID. A thread, by contrast, shares the address space with all the other threads in the same process. So IPC is what you need when you're crossing process boundaries; thread synchronization handles coordination within a single process."

Q: How do you communicate with a service in another process?

"You return an IBinder from Service.onBind(). The client receives a proxy object rather than the real thing, and each method call on that proxy becomes a Binder transaction that the kernel Binder driver routes over to the server process."

Q: How do you handle remote process death?

"You register an IBinder.DeathRecipient via binder.linkToDeath(recipient, 0). When the remote process dies, the binderDied() callback fires on a Binder thread, and from there you can attempt a rebind, surface an error to the user, or clean up any state you were holding. You should also implement ServiceConnection.onServiceDisconnected to cover the service binding lifecycle side of the same event."

5.2 Binder

Definition

Binder is Android's proprietary IPC mechanism — a Linux kernel driver at /dev/binder that enables lightweight, secure RPC between processes. It underpins virtually every Android API: ActivityManager, WindowManager, PackageManager, and every AIDL or Messenger call all go through Binder.

How it works internally

Client process                    Kernel (Binder driver)              Server process
──────────────                    ──────────────────────              ──────────────
IBinder.transact()  ─── data ───► /dev/binder                   ◄─── Binder.onTransact()
(blocks thread)                   copies once (shared mem)           (runs on Binder thread)
                    ◄── reply ───  wakes client thread

Unlike traditional UNIX IPC mechanisms like pipes, sockets, or shared memory, Binder achieves a single-copy transfer: data is written into a kernel-mapped buffer that is also mapped into the server's address space, so the kernel only copies once (client to kernel), not twice. This makes it significantly faster than UNIX domain sockets for small-to-medium messages.

There are three key properties worth knowing. First, identity: each Binder object has a unique kernel-level token, and the client holds a proxy rather than the real object (unless both sides are in the same process). Second, security: the kernel records the calling PID and UID via Binder.getCallingUid() and Binder.getCallingPid(), and these cannot be spoofed by userspace. Third, reference counting: the kernel tracks how many proxy holders exist, and when the last proxy is dropped, the Binder is garbage-collected on the server side.

Binder thread pool

Every process that uses Binder has a thread pool managed by ProcessState. The default pool size is 15 threads. Incoming transactions are dispatched to any idle thread in the pool. The main thread is never part of this pool — it has its own Looper.

Server process
├── main thread  (Looper — not in Binder pool)
├── Binder thread 1  ← handles incoming IPC call
├── Binder thread 2
└── Binder thread N  (up to 15)

If all Binder threads are busy — say they're all blocked waiting on a downstream service — new transactions queue up and the caller blocks until a thread becomes available. If that blocked caller happens to be the main thread, you get an ANR.

Synchronous vs asynchronous calls

Mode Behaviour Use when
Synchronous (default)Caller blocks until server returnsYou need a return value or confirmation
Asynchronous (oneway in AIDL)Caller returns immediately; server processes laterFire-and-forget; notifications

Synchronous Binder calls from the main thread are an ANR risk if the remote is slow. Always call from a background thread or use oneway.

Transaction size limits and TransactionTooLargeException

The Binder kernel buffer is roughly 1 MB per process, shared across all simultaneous transactions from and to that process. Each individual transaction payload is practically limited to around 500 KB, but the smaller the better.

// BAD — sending a large Bitmap over Binder
val bundle = Bundle()
bundle.putParcelable("image", largeBitmap)   // could be several MB
intent.putExtras(bundle)
startActivity(intent)                         // throws TransactionTooLargeException at runtime

TransactionTooLargeException is thrown in two situations: when a single transaction exceeds the 1 MB kernel buffer, or when the combined in-flight transactions to a process push past that limit. There are four ways to avoid it: pass file descriptors via ParcelFileDescriptor instead of raw bytes; write large data to disk or a ContentProvider and send a URI reference instead; use shared memory via MemoryFile or the SharedMemory API on API 27 and above; or chunk large payloads if you need to stream them.

What NOT to send over Binder

  • Large bitmaps or byte arrays — use ParcelFileDescriptor or a URI instead.
  • Serializable objects — they're slow and fragile; use Parcelable.
  • Database cursors — use the Cursor/ContentProvider API, which wraps them in BulkCursorToCursorAdaptor.
  • References to live objects — non-Binder Java objects simply cannot cross process boundaries.
  • Sensitive credentials in plaintext when you haven't yet validated the caller's UID.

RemoteException

Any method call on a remote IBinder proxy can throw RemoteException if the remote process has died. The most common subclass is DeadObjectException, which specifically means the remote Binder object is gone. Always catch RemoteException rather than just DeadObjectException, because other transport errors exist too.

try {
    remoteService.doWork()
} catch (e: RemoteException) {
    // Remote process is dead or unreachable
    Log.e(TAG, "Remote service died", e)
    rebindService()
}

Death recipients

class RemoteServiceClient {
    private var binder: IMyService? = null

    private val deathRecipient = IBinder.DeathRecipient {
        // Called on a Binder thread when the remote process dies
        binder = null
        mainHandler.post { reconnect() }
    }

    fun onServiceConnected(name: ComponentName, service: IBinder) {
        binder = IMyService.Stub.asInterface(service)
        // Register BEFORE first call — the process could die any time
        service.linkToDeath(deathRecipient, 0)
    }

    fun onServiceDisconnected(name: ComponentName) {
        // Called on main thread — unlink to avoid double-firing
        binder?.asBinder()?.unlinkToDeath(deathRecipient, 0)
        binder = null
    }

    fun reconnect() {
        bindService(intent, connection, Context.BIND_AUTO_CREATE)
    }
}

One critical detail: binderDied() fires on a Binder thread, not the main thread. If you need to update UI from it, post to a Handler or route through LiveData or StateFlow.

Avoid heavy work in Binder callbacks

Binder threads are a finite pool. If your onTransact implementation — or any AIDL method body — does heavy work like network I/O, database queries, or complex computation, you starve the pool and block all incoming IPC to that process, including system calls from ActivityManager.

The best practice is to dispatch heavy work to a coroutine or a separate thread pool immediately in the Binder callback, and return from the Binder thread as fast as possible.

// In AIDL Stub implementation — BAD
override fun processLargeData(data: ByteArray): Result {
    val result = database.runSlowQuery()  // blocks Binder thread
    return result
}

// GOOD — return a callback interface, or use oneway + callback pattern
override fun processLargeDataAsync(data: ByteArray, callback: IResultCallback) {
    scope.launch {
        val result = database.runSlowQuery()
        try { callback.onResult(result) } catch (e: RemoteException) { /* client died */ }
    }
}

Interview angles — Binder

Q: What is Binder?

"Binder is Android's kernel-level IPC driver. It enables RPC between processes using a single-copy data transfer, it gives you built-in caller identity through UID and PID, and it manages the lifecycle of remote objects with reference counting."

Q: What is a Binder thread?

"A Binder thread is a thread in the server process's pool that sits blocked inside ioctl(/dev/binder), waiting for incoming transactions. When a client calls a remote method, the kernel wakes one idle Binder thread to execute onTransact. Meanwhile, the calling thread on the client side stays blocked until the server returns — that's the synchronous mode."

Q: What happens if a Binder transaction blocks?

"The calling thread blocks indefinitely, or until a timeout if the kernel is using SYNC_WAIT. The critical case is when that blocked thread is the main thread: if the block exceeds 5 seconds for an Activity or 10 seconds for a Service, Android raises an ANR dialog. That's exactly why all synchronous IPC calls must go on a background thread unless the method is marked oneway."

Q: How do you design safe IPC APIs?

"There are six rules I follow. First, mark fire-and-forget calls as oneway in AIDL so the caller doesn't block. Second, use a callback or listener AIDL interface for results that come back from oneway calls. Third, always catch RemoteException — every remote call can throw it. Fourth, link death recipients immediately on bind, before you make any calls. Fifth, validate caller UID with Binder.getCallingUid() and never trust the client's self-reported identity. Sixth, keep transaction payloads small and use file descriptors for any bulk data."

5.3 AIDL

Definition

AIDL — Android Interface Definition Language — is Android's IDL for defining IPC interfaces. The AIDL compiler, either the standalone aidl tool or the Gradle plugin, generates Java and Kotlin boilerplate for you: a Stub abstract class on the server side that extends Binder, and a Proxy class on the client side that wraps IBinder.transact(). You define the contract in a .aidl file and the generated code handles all the marshalling and unmarshalling.

Supported types in AIDL

Category Types
Primitivesboolean, byte, char, short, int, long, float, double
StringsString, CharSequence
CollectionsList<T> (T must be AIDL-supported), Map (keys/values must be supported)
ParcelableAny class implementing Parcelable (must be declared in its own .aidl file)
Other interfacesOther AIDL interfaces
RawIBinder

Not supported natively: Serializable, arbitrary objects, or file streams — for those, use ParcelFileDescriptor.

Directional tags: in, out, inout

Parameters in AIDL methods have a directional tag that controls marshalling direction:

Tag Client → Server Server → Client Use when
in (default for primitives)Data copiedNot copied backClient sends, server reads only
outNot copied to serverCopied backClient provides empty container; server fills it
inoutCopied both waysCopied backBidirectional; most expensive

Primitives and String are always implicitly in. Objects require an explicit directional tag.

One-way (oneway) calls

Adding oneway to a method makes the client call non-blocking. The client returns immediately after the transaction is enqueued, and the server processes the call asynchronously on a Binder thread. The trade-offs are that oneway methods cannot have return values, and they cannot have out or inout parameters because there is no return path.

interface IEventService {
    oneway void logEvent(String name, in Bundle params);  // fire and forget
    int getEventCount();                                   // synchronous, blocks caller
}

If you mark an entire interface oneway, all methods in it become non-blocking.

Minimal AIDL example

File: app/src/main/aidl/com/example/ICalculator.aidl

// ICalculator.aidl
package com.example;

interface ICalculator {
    /** Synchronous call — caller blocks until result is returned. */
    int add(int a, int b);

    /** Fire-and-forget — caller returns immediately. */
    oneway void scheduleComputation(int jobId, in int[] operands);

    /** Passes a Parcelable in both directions. */
    ComputeResult compute(inout ComputeRequest request);
}

File: app/src/main/aidl/com/example/ComputeRequest.aidl

// Every Parcelable used in AIDL needs its own declaration file.
package com.example;
parcelable ComputeRequest;

Server-side Stub implementation:

class CalculatorService : Service() {

    private val binder = object : ICalculator.Stub() {
        override fun add(a: Int, b: Int): Int {
            // Binder thread — keep it fast or dispatch to a coroutine scope
            return a + b
        }

        override fun scheduleComputation(jobId: Int, operands: IntArray) {
            // oneway — no return value, caller already unblocked
            scope.launch { processJob(jobId, operands) }
        }

        override fun compute(request: ComputeRequest): ComputeResult {
            // Validate caller — never trust the client
            val callerUid = Binder.getCallingUid()
            require(isAuthorized(callerUid)) { "Unauthorized UID: $callerUid" }
            return performCompute(request)
        }
    }

    override fun onBind(intent: Intent): IBinder = binder
}

Client-side binding and usage:

class ClientActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private var calculator: ICalculator? = null

    private val connection = object : ServiceConnection {
        override fun onServiceConnected(name: ComponentName, service: IBinder) {
            calculator = ICalculator.Stub.asInterface(service)
            // Stub.asInterface: returns the Stub directly if same process,
            // or wraps it in a Proxy if cross-process.
            service.linkToDeath(deathRecipient, 0)
        }
        override fun onServiceDisconnected(name: ComponentName) {
            calculator = null
        }
    }

    private val deathRecipient = IBinder.DeathRecipient {
        calculator = null
        runOnUiThread { rebind() }
    }

    fun callRemote() {
        lifecycleScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {   // NEVER call from main thread
            try {
                val result = calculator?.add(3, 4) ?: return@launch
                withContext(Dispatchers.Main) { updateUi(result) }
            } catch (e: RemoteException) {
                Log.e(TAG, "Remote call failed", e)
            }
        }
    }
}

Versioning and backward compatibility

Binder is the backbone of platform services across Android versions, so breaking an AIDL interface is extremely disruptive. There are five rules to follow.

First, never remove or reorder methods. Method IDs are assigned by declaration order, so reordering breaks binary compatibility silently — calls dispatch to the wrong method with no compiler warning.

Second, add new methods at the end only. Old clients calling transact with an unrecognized method code receive UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION, which the Stub base class returns as false. Handle that gracefully.

Third, for stable AIDL interfaces you can provide default method bodies, which allows new methods to be added without breaking old clients that haven't implemented them yet.

Fourth, version the interface explicitly. The convention is a getVersion(): Int method, or the @VintfStability and @Backing annotations for HAL-level AIDL.

Fifth, for Parcelable evolution: add new fields with defaults, write a version integer as the first field in writeToParcel, and check that version number in createFromParcel before reading newer fields.

// Robust Parcelable that handles older versions
data class UserProfile(
    val id: String,
    val name: String,
    val email: String = ""   // added in v2 — must default for older senders
) : Parcelable {
    companion object CREATOR : Parcelable.Creator<UserProfile> {
        private const val VERSION = 2

        override fun createFromParcel(source: Parcel): UserProfile {
            val version = source.readInt()
            val id = source.readString()!!
            val name = source.readString()!!
            val email = if (version >= 2) source.readString()!! else ""
            return UserProfile(id, name, email)
        }
        override fun newArray(size: Int) = arrayOfNulls<UserProfile>(size)
    }

    override fun writeToParcel(dest: Parcel, flags: Int) {
        dest.writeInt(VERSION)
        dest.writeString(id)
        dest.writeString(name)
        dest.writeString(email)
    }
    override fun describeContents() = 0
}

Interview angles — AIDL

Q: When do you need AIDL?

"You reach for AIDL when you need typed, multi-method RPC between processes — specifically when you need return values, when you have multiple concurrent callers, or when you're passing complex object graphs. Concrete examples are a background processing service that returns results, an inter-app SDK, or a system service extension."

Q: AIDL vs Messenger?

See dedicated section below.

Q: Synchronous vs one-way AIDL?

"Synchronous means the caller blocks until the server returns, and you can have a return value. One-way means the caller returns immediately after enqueuing the transaction, but there's no return value possible. I use oneway for any event or notification call where I don't need a result back, because it completely eliminates the ANR risk on the caller side."

Q: How do you version IPC contracts?

"There are two parts to this. For the interface itself: add new methods at the end only, never remove or reorder existing ones, and add a getVersion(): Int method so callers can check what the server supports before calling new methods. For Parcelable types that go across the wire: write a version integer as the first field, and in createFromParcel check that version before reading any fields that were added after the initial version."

5.4 Messenger

Definition

Messenger is a simpler IPC mechanism built on top of Binder. It wraps a Handler in a Binder object, letting the remote process send Message objects to that Handler. Under the hood it still uses AIDL — Android ships IMessenger.aidl in the framework — but it hides all the marshalling complexity behind the familiar Message API.

How it works

Client process                         Server process
──────────────                         ──────────────
Messenger(service IBinder)             Handler handles messages sequentially
   └─ serverMessenger.send(msg)        └─ handleMessage(msg: Message)
        │                                       ▲
        └─── Binder IPC ──────────────────────►─┘
             (IMessenger.send transaction)
  1. The Service returns a Messenger's underlying IBinder from onBind().
  2. The client wraps that IBinder in Messenger(binder).
  3. The client calls serverMessenger.send(message).
  4. The Message is marshalled over Binder and delivered to the server's Handler.handleMessage().
  5. For replies, the client attaches replyTo = Messenger(clientHandler) to the message.

All messages are processed sequentially through the Handler's MessageQueue. There is no parallelism — the server handles one message at a time, by design.

Service skeleton

class MessengerService : Service() {

    private val incomingHandler = object : Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()) {
        override fun handleMessage(msg: Message) {
            when (msg.what) {
                MSG_COMPUTE -> {
                    val input = msg.data.getInt("value")
                    val result = input * 2

                    // Reply to client if replyTo is set
                    msg.replyTo?.let { replyMessenger ->
                        val reply = Message.obtain(null, MSG_RESULT)
                        reply.data = Bundle().apply { putInt("result", result) }
                        try {
                            replyMessenger.send(reply)
                        } catch (e: RemoteException) {
                            // Client died — ignore or clean up
                        }
                    }
                }
                else -> super.handleMessage(msg)
            }
        }
    }

    private val messenger = Messenger(incomingHandler)

    override fun onBind(intent: Intent): IBinder = messenger.binder

    companion object {
        const val MSG_COMPUTE = 1
        const val MSG_RESULT = 2
    }
}

Client skeleton

class MessengerClient : AppCompatActivity() {
    private var serverMessenger: Messenger? = null

    private val replyHandler = object : Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()) {
        override fun handleMessage(msg: Message) {
            if (msg.what == MessengerService.MSG_RESULT) {
                val result = msg.data.getInt("result")
                updateUi(result)
            }
        }
    }
    private val replyMessenger = Messenger(replyHandler)

    private val connection = object : ServiceConnection {
        override fun onServiceConnected(name: ComponentName, service: IBinder) {
            serverMessenger = Messenger(service)
        }
        override fun onServiceDisconnected(name: ComponentName) {
            serverMessenger = null
        }
    }

    fun sendRequest(value: Int) {
        val msg = Message.obtain(null, MessengerService.MSG_COMPUTE)
        msg.data = Bundle().apply { putInt("value", value) }
        msg.replyTo = replyMessenger   // attach reply channel
        try {
            serverMessenger?.send(msg)
        } catch (e: RemoteException) {
            Log.e(TAG, "Service not available", e)
        }
    }
}

Key characteristics

  • Sequential delivery: All messages queue through a single Handler, so there's no concurrent message processing. That's good for ordered operations but bad for high-throughput parallel work.
  • Message payload: Message.obj can hold any Parcelable. Message.data is a Bundle. Message.arg1 and arg2 are int fields for cheap primitives.
  • msg.what: An integer discriminator for the message type. You must define constants for all message types — there is no type safety here, unlike AIDL interfaces.
  • No return values: send() is always fire-and-forget. Replies require the client to attach a separate replyTo Messenger to the message.
  • Thread context: The Handler executes on whatever thread its Looper belongs to — usually the main thread. If message handling is heavy, back it with a HandlerThread instead.
// Using HandlerThread for background message processing
class HeavyMessengerService : Service() {
    private lateinit var handlerThread: HandlerThread

    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        handlerThread = HandlerThread("MessengerWorker").also { it.start() }
    }

    private val incomingHandler by lazy {
        object : Handler(handlerThread.looper) {
            override fun handleMessage(msg: Message) { /* heavy work ok here */ }
        }
    }

    private val messenger by lazy { Messenger(incomingHandler) }
    override fun onBind(intent: Intent): IBinder = messenger.binder

    override fun onDestroy() {
        handlerThread.quitSafely()
        super.onDestroy()
    }
}

Interview angles — Messenger

Q: Messenger vs AIDL?

See detailed table in the next section.

Q: When is Messenger enough?

"Messenger is the right call when your IPC is simple, sequential, and fire-and-forget — for example, a background download service where you just send it commands and don't need typed responses back. It's also good for prototyping or when you need cross-process event delivery but don't want to deal with generating and maintaining AIDL stubs."

Q: Why is Messenger simpler but less flexible?

"Because everything goes through a single Handler and MessageQueue. There are no return values, no parallel processing, and no typed method signatures — every message is an integer code in msg.what, which is untyped and error-prone. And it fundamentally can't express 'give me back a result synchronously.' If you need a reply, you have to attach a replyTo Messenger to every message and handle the response asynchronously on the other end. That overhead is fine for simple command-style patterns, but the moment you need a real typed API with return values, you've outgrown Messenger."

Parcelable vs Serializable

Parcelable versus Serializable comes up in almost every Binder or IPC interview question, so it's worth having a crisp answer ready.

Dimension Parcelable Serializable
Locationandroid.os.Parcelablejava.io.Serializable
MechanismManual implementation — you control every field written/readJava reflection + serialization protocol
Performance~10x faster for IPC; minimal allocationsSlow — creates many temporary objects; reflection overhead
MemoryWrites to Parcel (shared memory / kernel buffer)Writes to ObjectOutputStream byte stream
Suitable for IPCYes — designed for BinderNo — not designed for Binder; technically works but discouraged
BoilerplateMedium (mitigated with @Parcelize plugin)None — just implements Serializable
VersioningManual — must handle evolution explicitlyserialVersionUID — fragile
PersistenceNot intended for disk persistence (Parcel format is not stable across Android versions)Intended for disk/network persistence
@Parcelize@Parcelize annotation + kotlin-parcelize plugin generates implementationN/A
// Parcelable with @Parcelize — no boilerplate
@Parcelize
data class Doctor(
    val id: String,
    val name: String,
    val specialty: String,
    val rating: Float
) : Parcelable

The recommendation is straightforward: always use Parcelable for anything passed over Binder — Intent extras, Bundle contents, AIDL parameters. Use Serializable only when you need cross-JVM disk persistence and performance is not critical.

One thing worth calling out specifically: Parcelable is not safe for disk persistence. The Parcel binary format is internal to Android and can change between OS versions — a Parcel written on Android 12 might be unreadable on Android 14. For persistence, use Room, DataStore, or JSON/Protobuf.

AIDL vs Messenger Decision Guide

Criterion Use AIDL Use Messenger
Need typed method callsYesNo — only msg.what integers
Need return valuesYesNo — always async via replyTo
Need concurrent/parallel processingYes — Binder thread pool handles concurrent callsNo — single Handler serializes all
ComplexityHigher — generate stubs, handle exceptionsLower — familiar Handler/Message API
Type safetyYes — compiler enforces method signaturesNo — integer codes, unchecked Bundle
Performance (high throughput)BetterWorse — sequential queue
Callback interfacesNative — define callback AIDLAwkward — need a separate reply Messenger
Best forSDK-style service API, system services, complex bidirectional IPCSimple command service, ordered event delivery, quick prototyping

The rule of thumb is: start with Messenger if you just need to send commands to a background service. Upgrade to AIDL when you need return values, typed interfaces, or concurrent call handling.

Interview Quick-Reference

Question One-line answer
What is Binder?Android's kernel IPC driver enabling single-copy RPC with caller identity verification
What is a Binder thread?A thread in the Binder pool blocked on /dev/binder, awakened to handle incoming transactions
What causes TransactionTooLargeException?Transaction payload exceeds ~1 MB kernel buffer; use file descriptors or URIs for large data
What is oneway in AIDL?Makes a method non-blocking — caller returns immediately, no return value allowed
What is a death recipient?IBinder.DeathRecipient callback fired on a Binder thread when the remote process dies
Parcelable vs Serializable?Parcelable is ~10x faster, designed for Binder; Serializable is reflection-based, not safe for IPC
AIDL vs Messenger?AIDL = typed, concurrent, return values; Messenger = simple, sequential, fire-and-forget
Static variables across processes?Not shared — each process has an independent JVM instance
Can you call AIDL from main thread?Only oneway methods are safe; synchronous calls risk ANR — use background threads
How do you secure a Binder interface?Call Binder.getCallingUid() and validate against expected UID / permission check
What data should NOT cross Binder?Large bitmaps, Serializable objects, raw file streams, arbitrary object references
How do you version AIDL?Add methods at the end only, never remove/reorder; add getVersion() method
